The Committee highlights strong labor markets and solid household spending but acknowledges weak business fixed investment and exports and inflation running below 2%. Academic evidence suggests this policy mix is appropriate: firms’ investment—especially inventories—can be constrained by internal finance and liquidity conditions (Kashyap, Lamont, and Stein, 1994), so the rate cut alongside Treasury bill purchases and repo operations should ease money-market pressures and support investment spending. Empirical VAR studies show monetary policy shocks have measurable real effects (e.g., Sims, 1992), reinforcing the case for preemptive easing amid global uncertainty. With inflation and market-based inflation compensation low, expectations become pivotal; New Keynesian analyses emphasize the role of expected inflation in current inflation dynamics (Galí, Gertler, and López-Salido), and inflation-forecast targeting arguments (Svensson) support accommodation to guide inflation back to the symmetric 2% objective. Overall, the stance is cautiously supportive of continued expansion, with clear acknowledgement of downside risks.
